2.3.2.1 Quality Target Product Profile

The Quality Target Product Profile (QTPP) provided in Table 1 describes the elements related to quality, safety and efficacy.

Table 1. Quality Target Product Profile and Associated Quality Attributes
Product Quality AttributeTarget
Route of Administration and Dosage FormOral film-coated tablet
Dose Strength(s)20 mg
PotencyMeet pharmacopoeia requirements for identity, assay and content uniformity
In vitro Drug ReleaseImmediate release
Degradants and ImpuritiesControlled in accordance with ICH Q3 and M7 guidelines; regional guidelines for nitrosamine impurities, as applicable

Shelf Life36 months at room temperature across all climatic zones

2.3.2.1.1 Critical Quality Attributes

Identification of critical quality attributes from the QTPP was based on the severity of harm to a patient (safety and efficacy) resulting from failure to meet the acceptance criteria for each quality attribute. Investigation during pharmaceutical development focused on those CQAs that could be impacted by a realistic change to the drug product formulation or drug substance or drug product manufacturing process (see Table 2).

Table 2 Critical Quality Attributes
Quality attributeJustification
Drug Product DescriptionColor, shape and appearance are not directly linked to safety and efficacy, but can indirectly impact through medication errors, patient compliance, dose identification, etc. The target is set to ensure product quality and patient acceptability.
Drug Product IdentificationThough identification is critical for safety and efficacy, this CQA can be effectively controlled by the quality management system and will be monitored at drug product release.
Drug Product Uniformity of Dosage UnitsVariability in content uniformity will affect safety and efficacy. Both formulation and process variables impact content uniformity, so this CQA will be evaluated throughout product and process development.
Drug Product AssayAssay variability will affect safety and efficacy. Process variables may affect the assay of the drug product.
Drug Product DissolutionFailure to meet the dissolution specification can impact bioavailability. Formulation, material attributes and process variables affect the dissolution profile.
Drug Product ImpuritiesImpurities in the drug product can affect safety and are controlled to levels demonstrated to be safe per ICH Q3 and ICH M7, which enable routine manufacturing to ensure a robust supply for patients.
Microbiological QualityControl of microbiological quality ensures patient safety

2.3.2.2 Overall Development Strategy

SakuraBloom is an immediate-release 20 mg film-coated tablet, manufactured via wet granulation followed by compression and film coating.

The development followed a systematic Quality by Design (QbD) approach, in alignment with ICH Q8, Q9 and Q11. The drug substance (API), Sakuramil, is a poorly soluble, highly permeable BCS Class II compound manufactured with proprietary technology from Sakura Pharmaceuticals Company, LTD (applicant), the same company that developed the finished product. Development and manufacture of the drug substance and drug product were performed at contract development and commercial manufacturers, IROHA-Corp and Aparna Pharmaceutical Manufacturing, respectively. This facilitated alignment between API and drug product development and ensured consistent control of critical material attributes (CMAs) throughout the manufacturing chain (from drug substance to finished product).

For the drug substance, particle size was identified as a CQA influencing dissolution and uniformity of dosage units. Controls were implemented within the release specifications and maintained through development and commercial manufacturing (see 2.3.4.DS.C and 2.3.4.DS.M). Key control elements included limits for related substances (e.g., CP-9-1, CP-8), potentially mutagenic impurities (e.g., CP-6), and residual solvents (Methylene chloride). Types and grade of excipients were chosen based on excipient compatibility studies (see 2.3.4.DP.D.1 Components of the drug product).

For the drug product, a design space was defined linking drug substance particle size distribution (PSD), granulation endpoint (granule particle size), and compression force, supported by DoE studies. Fluid bed granulation was selected to avoid thermal degradation risks. In-process controls – covering moisture content, particle size distribution, hardness, weight, and assay – ensure manufacturing robustness (see 2.3.4.DP.M). In the final control strategy of the drug product, granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness are controlled within a design space to ensure satisfactory dissolution. The developed in-house dissolution method (2.3.3 AP (Dissolution/UV}) is capable of differentiating between formulations manufactured using different PSD of the drug substance and predicting their in vivo performance in the pilot bioequivalence (BE) study. Film coating is controlled to ensure uniform appearance. Control strategies integrate in-process monitoring/RTRT and specification testing, ensuring the intended product quality at release and throughout shelf life (see 2.3.3.DP.C).

2.3.2.3 Overall Control Strategy Summary Representation

Enhanced understanding has been obtained through development. The Fishbone diagram (Figure 1) shows an overview of the drug product CQAs in the context of an integrated drug substance and drug product overall control strategy, including process design, CPPs, CMAs and critical IPCs.

Figure 1. Fishbone Diagram of Overall Control Strategy for Sakura Bloom.

[IMAGE: Sakura_Bloom_OCS_Fishbone.png]

<Double click image to enlarge>

A simplified flowchart diagram depicting the overall control strategy illustrates which elements are responsible for ensuring that each CQA is met, and where the relevant parameters and material attributes are controlled in the overall control strategy (see Figure 2). These diagrams demonstrates how the control strategy, which consists of the process controls and material controls for the raw materials, intermediates, and final product, ensures the quality, safety, and efficacy of the product throughout the product life cycle, and supports the concept of ongoing process verification and continual improvement.

Figure 2. Overall Control Strategy for Sakura Bloom.

[IMAGE: 0_0]

<Double click image to enlarge>

The overall control strategy is also summarized in Table 3. The control strategy summary table illustrates which elements are responsible for ensuring that each CQA is met, and where the relevant parameters and material attributes are controlled in the overall control strategy. The first column lists the product attribute.  The second column lists the CQA.  The third column provides functional relationships between the CQA and the elements of the control strategy, and the fourth column lists the controls that appear in the PLCM/registration elements. The control types are categorized as follows:

• Design - Controls implicit in the design of the manufacturing process (e.g., sequence of

purification steps or order of addition)

• CMA - Controls on material attributes (including raw materials, starting materials,

intermediates, reagents, primary packaging materials, etc.)

• CPP - Critical process parameter

• IPC - In-process controls (including in-process tests and process parameters)

• Spec - Controls on the product specification (e.g., release testing/stability testing).

The fifth column provides a brief description of the control. It should be noted that additional GMP controls are in place and are documented in the batch records and other GMP systems.

1 Manufacturing process

The Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet manufacturing process involves pre-blending, granulation, blending, compression, coating, inspection and packaging. Detailed information, e.g. all process parameters, is provided in [[3.2.DP.M Manufacture (Sakura Bloom) [APM][FCT][20 mg]]].

Pre-Blending

• Blend 52.000 kg of cellulose, microcrystalline, 26.000 kg of croscarmellose sodium, 353.600 kg of lactose monohydrate/Lactose hydrate and 52.000 kg of Sakuramil drug substance into a diffusion mixer (bin blender).

• Dissolve 15.600 kg hydroxypropyl cellulose in purified water using a vessel with stirrer to prepare a granulation liquid free from lumps.

Granulation and blending

• Load the pre-blended material from Step 1 into a fluid bed granulator and add granulation liquid from Step 2 using an inlet air volume of 40-45 m³/min, an inlet air temperature of 75-85°C and a spray rate of 900 – 1100 g/min, to achieve wetting of pre-blended material and formation of granules.

• Dry the obtained granules using dryer integrated within the fluid bed granulator unit. until loss on drying of 1 - 2% is achieved.

• Sieve the dried granules from Step 4 using a screening mill.

• Sieve 5.200 kg of magnesium stearate through a screen and add it to the granules from Step 5.

• Blend the mixture from step 6 using a diffusion mixer (bin blender) to obtain the final blend.

Tablet compression

• Compress the final blend from step 7 using a tablet press at 20-30 revolutions with a compression force of 6-14 kN to obtain the tablet cores.

Film-coating

• Prepare a homogeneous suspension of the Basic coating premix, red in purified water in a suitable sized vessel.

• Film-coat the tablet cores from Step 8 using the film coat suspension from Step 9 in a coating pan to achieve desired film-coat weight gain, followed by drying. Collect the film coated tablets in a suitable container.

Inspection

• Collect 10 tablets to perform Description test method with RTRT and Identification Test method with RTRT.

Packaging

• The film-coated tablets are primary packaged.

• The primary packaged product is then packed in a cardboard based secondary pack.

Information on the characterization

The CP-9 identification standard, batch no. SAKU_ID_Std_04, was prepared in-house by spiking a selected batch of Sakuramil with known impurities CP-9-1 and CP-8. This mixture is used for the determination of related substances by HPLC. The identification standard and its constituent impurities were fully characterized using in-house analytical methods, including mass spectrometry, ^1H NMR, and ^13C NMR. This confirms the suitability of the CP-9 identification standard for its intended analytical application.

2.3.4.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

This summary includes the tested performance characteristics, acceptance criteria, and results of validation. 2.3.4.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development

• Objective

To develop a Near-Infrared (NIR) spectroscopy method for the identification and assay of Excipient A and API B in a solid oral dosage form.

2. Product Description

The product is a solid tablet containing API B (50 mg) and Excipient A (filler), along with other excipients.

3. Instrumentation

FT-NIR Spectrometer equipped with an integrating sphere or fiber optic probe.

4. Method Parameters

Wavelength Range: 1000–2500 nm

Resolution: 8 cm⁻¹

Number of Scans: 64 scans per sample

5. Sample Preparation

For Identification: Direct scan of intact tablet or powder.

For Assay: Powdered blend homogenized before scanning.

6. Reference Standards

Certified reference standards of Excipient A and API B, and a placebo blend.

7. Calibration Model (Assay)

Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression using known concentrations of API B.

8. Preprocessing Techniques

Multiplicative Scatter Correction (MSC), First derivative, and Smoothing (Savitzky-Golay).

9. Validation Parameters

Specificity, Linearity, Accuracy, Precision, Robustness, LOD/LOQ, and System Suitability.

Assay: Recovery 98–102%; R² ≥ 0.99 for calibration model.

11. System Suitability

Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) ≥ 100:1; consistent spectrum of standard.

12. Software Used

Chemometric software such as OPUS, Unscrambler, or TQ Analyst.

13. Challenges Addressed

Overlapping peaks of excipients, moisture interference, and tablet surface variability.

2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification

Appearance is a general requirement for dosage forms that ensures conformance to all of its distinguishable descriptive attributes.

The appearance of the film-coated tablets is tested by visual examination and must comply with the acceptance criteria. Appearance is a general requirement for dosage forms which ensures conformance of the dosage unit to all of its distinguishable descriptive attributes. Appearance testing detects potential visual defects and changes in physical aspects of the film-coated tablets which might occur during manufacturing or storage.

2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification

A feedforward control will be performed as an operation in commercial production so that the dissolution rate is about 90%. In other words, a control to keep the predicted dissolution value being always constant will be made by appropriately determining the target value for a granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness within this design space according to the particle size of drug substance.

The particle size of drug substance is measured as a specification testing in the process of drug substance, by a laser diffraction-scattering type particle size distribution measuring device. Without preparing samples for measurement, the powder of drug substance is measured for particle distribution by the dry method (specification testing of drug substance). Regarding the particle size of the granulation, the particle size at the end of granulation, which is obtained by a FBRM method is used. The uncoated tablet hardness is measured in 200 tablets (10 tablets over 20 time points) sampled over time.

2.3.4.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development

The development of a Real-Time Release Testing (RTRT) method using UV spectroscopy for dissolution monitoring demonstrates a robust, efficient, and science-based approach to pharmaceutical quality assurance. By leveraging in-line or on-line UV absorbance measurements, this method enables real-time prediction of dissolution performance, reducing reliance on traditional, time-consuming offline testing.

The integration of UV spectroscopy with appropriate calibration models and process controls ensures consistent product quality and supports continuous manufacturing initiatives. This RTRT strategy aligns with regulatory expectations for Process Analytical Technology (PAT) and Quality by Design (QbD), offering enhanced process understanding, faster batch release, and improved operational efficiency.

For further details, refer to [[3.2.AP Analytical Procedures (Dissolution/RTRT)[Performance][Sakura Bloom 20 mg]]]

2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification

Dissolution testing is performed in accordance with the Ph. Eur. 2.9.3 “Dissolution test for solid dosage forms”, Acceptance Table 1 of USP <711> “Dissolution”, or JP <6.10> “Dissolution test” (harmonized method), using the paddle method (apparatus 2) at 50 ± 2 rpm and 900 mL of 4.0 N McIlvaine buffer as the dissolution medium. The USP apparatus 2 (paddle) method was chosen based on the dosage form.

Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet is an immediate release product. The speed of 50 rpm is considered standard for the paddle apparatus to provide agitation for an immediate release product. The setting of Q-value and Q-time is based on the release and stability data obtained for batch ABC123 used in registration stability. It was established to ensure that sufficient in vitro release can be achieved. No other batches of Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablet were used in clinical trials in support of this marketing authorization application. Nevertheless, the requirements previously mentioned are also supported by the dissolution data obtained for the registration stability batches ABC123 and ABC456. The specifications follow the Acceptance Table 1 of USP <711> “Dissolution”, Ph. Eur. 2.9.3 “Dissolution test for solid dosage forms”, JP <6.10> “Dissolution test” (harmonized method) for S1 and S2 testing for release and for stages 1, 2 and 3 for stability. This test is performed at release and during stability.

A detailed discussion on the choice of the dissolution method as well as dissolution profile data for these batches are provided in [[2.1 Dissolution testing]].

Comparative testing using USP Apparatus I (Basket) and II (Paddle) was performed. Apparatus II (Paddle) at 50 ± 2 rpm provided consistent and reproducible results with minimal variability.

During the development phase, sampling timepoints of 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, and 45 were set to adequately characterize the ascending and plateau phases of the dissolution curves. More than 85% of the drug is released within the duration of the dissolution test.

Medium deaeration was evaluated and showed no impact on dissolution. Batches with original formulation, medium with deliberate formulation (e.g. (such as higher magnesium stearate) and process variation (such as larger API particle size) were tested, showing distinct dissolution behaviors under different conditions. Therefore, The method’s discriminatory capability was demonstrated.

The finalized dissolution method for Sakura Bloom 20 mg as depicted in [[2.3.3. AP Analytical Procedures (Dissolution/UV)[Performance][Sakura Bloom 20 mg]]] is scientifically justified, robust, and compliant with international pharmacopoeial standards. It demonstrates reproducibility, discriminatory power, and suitability for routine quality control, comparative dissolution studies, and regulatory submissions. The incorporation of UV detection and McIlvaine buffer at pH 5.0 ensures reliable performance and sensitivity across batches, supporting product quality throughout its shelf life.

For details and raw data of method development, please refer to [[3.2.AP Analytical Procedures (Dissolution/UV)[Performance][Sakura Bloom 20 mg]]].

Microbiological Examination of Non-Sterile Products: Tests for Specified Micro-Organisms”.

MET is proposed to be performed as a frequency test (periodic quality indicator test). The risk of microbial contamination of the drug product is considered low due to the manufacturing process, environmental monitoring, and cleaning procedures in place. The entire process is a dry granulation, blending and compression, and does not use any water or other microbial-growth supporting solvents, except during the coating step.

Water activity results of less than 0.2 for the final blend, uncoated and coated tablets (Table 1 and Table 2), as well as the historical MET data supports this assessment (Table 3 and Table 4). During development, microbial enumeration testing was performed on 3 pilot-scale/registration stability batches (i.e., ABC123, ABC456 and ABC789). For all batches tested to date, the results met the proposed requirements. Furthermore, no microbial growth was observed at 6-month registration stability testing point in either blister packaging under accelerated conditions (Table 4).

Therefore, the proposal to perform MET as frequency test is consistent with the ICH guideline Q6A (Decision tree #8). The microbial enumeration tests will be performed at release on the first 5 consecutive production batches. If the requirements are met, testing frequency may be reduced to every 10th batch. At least one batch will be tested in each calendar year in which the product is manufactured.

2.3.4.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development

• Objective

To develop a Near-Infrared (NIR) spectroscopy method for the identification and assay of Excipient A and API B in a solid oral dosage form.

2. Product Description

The product is a solid tablet containing API B (50 mg) and Excipient A (filler), along with other excipients.

3. Instrumentation

FT-NIR Spectrometer equipped with an integrating sphere or fiber optic probe.

4. Method Parameters

Wavelength Range: 1000–2500 nm

Resolution: 8 cm⁻¹

Number of Scans: 64 scans per sample

5. Sample Preparation

For Identification: Direct scan of intact tablet or powder.

For Assay: Powdered blend homogenized before scanning.

6. Reference Standards

Certified reference standards of Excipient A and API B, and a placebo blend.

7. Calibration Model (Assay)

Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression using known concentrations of API B.

8. Preprocessing Techniques

Multiplicative Scatter Correction (MSC), First derivative, and Smoothing (Savitzky-Golay).

9. Validation Parameters

Specificity, Linearity, Accuracy, Precision, Robustness, LOD/LOQ, and System Suitability.

10. Identification and Assay Criteria

Identification: Correlation coefficient ≥ 0.95 with reference spectrum.

Assay: Recovery 98–102%; R² ≥ 0.99 for calibration model.

11. System Suitability

Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) ≥ 100:1; consistent spectrum of standard.

12. Software Used

Chemometric software such as OPUS, Unscrambler, or TQ Analyst.

13. Challenges Addressed

Overlapping peaks of excipients, moisture interference, and tablet surface variability.

Risk evaluation of Nitrosamine impurities in Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet

The risk evaluation for the potential presence of Nitrosamine impurities, belonging to the mutagenic impurity cohort of concern (CoC) according to the ICH M7 guideline, has been performed.

The risk evaluation for Nitrosamine impurities follows the guidelines indicated below and is also

aligned with the requirements of further National Competent Authorities globally:

• Assessment report Article 5(3) of Regulation EC (No) 726/2004 ‘Nitrosamine impurities

in human medicinal products’ (EMA/369136/2020) and ‘Questions and answers for

marketing authorization holders/applicants on the CHMP Opinion for the Article 5(3) of

Regulation (EC) No 726/2004 referral on nitrosamine impurities in human medicinal

products’ (EMA/409815/2020, current revision).

• FDA Control of Nitrosamine Impurities in Human Drugs, Guidance for Industry, current

version

The contribution of the following factors to the potential presence of Nitrosamine impurities in

medicinal product are evaluated regarding:

The materials and their quality:

• Drug substance

• Drug product manufacturing process;

• excipients;

• primary packaging material(s).

Drug substance

The risk evaluation for the potential presence of Nitrosamine impurities due to the drug substance

(DS) process is documented in the drug substance risk evaluation [[2.1.2 Nitrosamine impurities]]

CP-6, which contains a secondary amine moiety, is included in the final API specification with a limit of NMT 37.5 ppm.

Excipients

The excipients used in the drug product were evaluated for their potential contribution to the

presence / formation of Nitrosamine impurities in the drug product. Table 2 below assesses the

excipients based on their structure and the potential contribution that they can have on formation

of N-nitroso compounds in the drug product.

Table 2 : Drug Product Excipients and Potential Contribution to Nitrosamine impurities presence / formation in the Drug Product Manufacturing Process

DescriptionExcipient
Excipients that neither have a structural alert for the presence or formation of N-nitrosamines, nor have risk for presence of vulnerable amines, but for which the presence of the nitrosating agent nitrite cannot be excluded. Based on available data on nitrite levels in excipients, the levels of reactive impurities such as nitrite are generally expected to be less than 10 ppm. These excipients can contribute to the risk of N-nitrosamine formation. These excipients have to be considered, in cases the API is reactive to trace amounts of nitrite and the nitrosation reaction is possible under the DP process conditions.Lactose monohydrate Microcrystalline cellulose Croscarmellose sodium Hydroxypropyl cellulose Magnesium stearate
Excipients that do not have a structural alert for the presence or formation of N-nitrosamines.Coating premix red

Drug Product Manufacturing Process

No nitrosating reagents are used in the process on drug

product equipment at the manufacturing site facility. No recycled or recovered materials are

used. The drug product equipment is not passivated with nitric acid or cleaned with chlorine or

chloramine. There are no nitrosating agents or nitrosamines that could be in contact with the

product during the manufacturing process.

There is a theoretical potential risk of nitrosamine impurity formation in the wet

granulation/drying process, where the API is initially suspended in water and afterwards the

wet granulated mass is dried by heating. Nonetheless, heat introduced during the drying phase

drives water evaporation, and the process is controlled to stop drying upon achievement of loss

on drying (LOD) limit.

Although CP-6 is controlled in the drug substance at tight limit of 37.5 ppm, during drug product manufacturing in presence of nitrosating agent precursors (e.g. nitrites from the excipients) there exists a potential theoretical risk for conversion to the respective Nitrosamine impurity N-Nitroso-CP-6 . Testing performed on three recent representative, production-scale and commercial batches (including samples of three batches stored under accelerated stability conditions) applying a quantification limit down to 10% of the acceptable intake (AI) limit however confirmed the absence.

Primary packaging material(s).

The current drug product primary packaging material consists of a HDPE bottle with desiccant

with polypropylene (PP) child resistant closure cap (or) PA/AL/PVC blister. There is no risk of Nitrosamine impurities formation / contamination of the drug product from the primary packaging material and process. There is also no risk from interaction of the solid dosage form with the primary packaging.

Risk of Increase/Formation of N-nitroso compounds during Storage

Based on 6 months accelerated stability at 40°C/75% RH available for 6 batches, there is no risk of increase/formation of Nitrosamine impurities during stability

Based on this evaluation, there is no risk for the presence of N-nitroso compounds (N-Nitroso-CP-6) in Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablet. The detailed risk evaluation including vendor assessments risk evaluation for Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablet is provided in [[3.2.DP.C.2 Justification of specifications]] .

PAT (Process analytical technology) - RTRT strategy justification

This document provides a scientific and regulatory justification for the implementation of Real-Time Release Testing (RTRT) for Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet. The proposed RTRT strategy complements end-product testing with in-process controls and predictive models, ensuring consistent product quality and compliance with regulatory expectations.

---

1. RTRT Scope and Strategy

---

RTRT will be applied to the following critical quality attributes (CQAs). The other CQA remains subject to conventional end-product testing.

CQARTRT MethodologyTraditional Method Replaced
IdentificationNIR spectroscopy during compressionHPLC
Content UniformityNIR spectroscopy during blendingUniformity of dosage units
DissolutionPredictive model based on process dataUSP dissolution test

In case of RTRT unavailability or model failure, conventional methods will be applied as a fallback approach.

---

2. Scientific Justification
2.1 Process Understanding

Extensive development studies have established a robust design space for blending, granulation, and compression. Critical process parameters (CPPs) are tightly controlled and correlated with CQAs. Risk assessments (ICH Q9) confirm confirm that the RTRT approach is commensurate with the level of process knowledge established during development.

2.2 Analytical Technology

• NIR Spectroscopy: Validated for quantitative assay and uniformity.

• Compression Force Sensors: Provide real-time feedback on tablet hardness and weight.

• Multivariate Models: Chemometric models predict dissolution profiles with high accuracy.

Calibration, maintenance, and data integrity measures are implemented to ensure robustness of PAT tools and multivariate models.

• Model lifecycle management includes periodic revalidation and performance monitoring.

1.1 Excipients screening and selection

Excipients for formulation development were selected based on the excipient compatibility results, functionality of excipients (e.g., binder, diluent,  disintegrant, lubricant etc.), the selected manufacturing process and available stability data. Excipient screening was conducted using different mixtures of diluent, binder, disintegrant and lubricant and these mixtures representing excipient blends suitable for wet granulation technology were blended with drug substance and stored for 6 weeks at open and closed conditions at 40°C/75%RH.

A discussion on rationale for selection of each excipient is summarized in the following sections.

Diluent / filling agents

Several diluents (filling agents) including lactose hydrate, D- mannitol and microcrystalline cellulose were evaluated for dissolution and hardness. The results showed that a combination of lactose hydrate and microcrystalline cellulose produced a formulation with the highest dissolution rate and appropriate hardness, therefore lactose hydrate and microcrystalline cellulose were selected as diluents.

Disintegrant

To select a disintegrant, croscarmellose sodium, crospovidone, carmellose calcium and low substituted hydroxypropyl cellulose were evaluated for dissolution. Croscarmellose sodium proved to be the most effective disintegrant because of its rapid dissolution and was added to the inner phase of the granulate only.

Binder

Hydroxypropyl cellulose was selected as a binder to aid the wet granulation process. It was selected over other binders based upon functional performance and preferable final drug product stability.

Lubricant

Magnesium stearate is a commonly used and effective lubricant. The selected levels have been proven to provide good physical characteristics of the tablets.

Film-coating

Hypromellose, macrogol and titanium oxide are commonly used coating components which have been shown not to interfere with the stability of the drug substance and to provide a smooth and glossy film coat.  To give an appearance of a pale red color, red ferric oxide was added as coloring agent.

3 Key physicochemical properties of drug substance influencing the performance of the drug product

Polymorphism

Only one drug substance polymorph was found to be obtained by the manufacturing process of the drug substance. The polymorphic form was monitored by X-ray powder diffraction method during drug product manufacturing. The polymorphic form was shown to be stable after wet granulation and fluid bed drying process. No change to the polymorphic form was identified during long-term storage in the intended primary packaging configuration of the drug product. Diffractograms to confirm the polymorphic form stability in the drug product are provided in [[3.2.DP.D.1 Components of the drug product]]

XRPD analysis of Sakurabloom 20 mg FCT across stability time points till end of Shelf-life (initial, 3 months, and 6 months, 24 months) under ICH conditions (25°C/60% RH, 30°C/75% RH and 40°C/75% RH) showed consistent diffraction peaks at 2θ values of 12.3°, 18.7°, 22.5°, 27.1°, 29.8 ° confirming the retention of the same crystalline polymorph. No peak shifts, broadening, or new peaks were observed, indicating polymorphic stability.

Particle size

The particle size for the drug substance is determined by laser light diffraction and the requirements are as follows: d (0.1) 26 nm, d (0.5) 40 nm and d (0.9) 66 nm. The drug substance with the same particle size distribution has been used throughout the drug product development and will be used in the commercial drug product manufacturing.

Water content

Sakuramil drug substance is non-hygroscopic. Water content (Loss on drying) test is routinely performed on the drug substance.

Sakuramil drug substance was subjected to stress testing at 40°C/75% RH for 30 days. Gravimetric analysis showed a negligible weight gain of <0.05%, and Karl Fischer titration confirmed moisture uptake below 0.1%. No physical changes (e.g., clumping, discoloration) were observed, supporting its classification as non-hygroscopic.

BCS classification

Based on the solubility profile across the physiological pH and based on the measured permeability across Caco-2 cell membranes ([[3.2.DP.D.1 Components of the drug product]]) , Sakuramil is considered to have low solubility and high permeability according to the Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS). Sakuramil is therefore classified as BCS Class 2 compound.

2.3.4.DP.D.2 Formulation development

1 Formulation development strategy

A systematic Quality by Design (QbD) approach was employed for formulation development of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet. With the prior knowledge on the drug substance and drug product and manufacturing experiences, Design of Experiments (DoE) and quality risk management were used. This enhanced approach to formulation and process development, enabled identification of Critical Quality Attributes (CQAs) and Critical Process Parameters (CPPs) of the drug substance and the drug product, and Real Time Release Testing (RTRT), supporting continual improvement throughout the product lifecycle.

Approach

Following approaches were employed to support definition of the control strategy for the final manufacturing process and quality assurance of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet.

• Establishment of the Quality Target Product Profile (QTPP) and initial risk assessment

• Identification of the product CQAs that ensure desired quality, safety and efficacy

• Assessment of the effects of the potential critical material attributes (p-CMA) on CQAs, and identification of critical material attributes (CMA)

• Assessment of the effects of potential critical process parameter (p-CPP) like inlet air volume, inlet air temperature, spray rate and tableting rotation speed on CMAs, and identification of critical process parameters (CPP)

• Construction of the control strategy

• Review of the risk assessment after implementation of the control strategy

• Overall evaluation of risk assessment

According to the approach described above, Preliminary Hazard Analysis (PHA) was used in the initial risk assessment, and Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) was used in the risk assessment of the manufacturing process and in the risk assessment after implementation of the control strategy. More information related to manufacturing is available at: [[1.2. Determination of CMAs affecting each CQA]]

A risk assessment based on the results of formulation development with Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet indicated that drug substance particle size, granule particle size, uncoated tablet hardness, uncoated tablet weight, uncoated tablet weight variation, and granule segregation impacted the drug product CQAs of dissolution, uniformity of dosage units, and assay. These attributes were therefore identified as CMAs. In the final control strategy, drug substance particle size was included in the specifications of the drug substance, granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness were to be controlled within the design space to ensure the dissolution, and uncoated tablet weight and the weight variation were to be controlled by in-process control. To confirm that the granule segregation is within the acceptable range, the drug substance concentrations in uncoated tablets are periodically monitored with near infrared spectrophotometry (NIR). CPPs in each unit operation were to be feedback-controlled with Process Analytical Technology (PAT) for granule particle size in the granulation process, and for uncoated tablet hardness, uncoated tablet weight, uncoated tablet weight variation and drug substance concentrations in uncoated tablets in the tableting process. Application of the above control strategy, including supporting models enables real time release testing for the drug product CQAs of dissolution, uniformity of dosage units, and assay.

2 Overages

No overage of Sakuramil is used in the formulation and manufacture of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets.

2.3.4.DP.M.1 Development of manufacturing process and process controls

1. Manufacturing process development

The same manufacturing process was used from the early development stage through to commercial supply. The process consists of the following steps:

Process 1 (granulation): granulation and drying using a fluid bed granulator

Process 2 (blending): mixing the granules and lubricant

Process 3 (tableting): compressing the blend to produce tablets,

Process 4 (coating),

Process 5 (inspection) and

Process 6 (packaging).

The equipment used for each process was identical to or the same principle as the equipment to be used for commercial production. Drug substance milling was performed as part of the manufacturing process of the drug substance.

To ensure the desired quality, safety, and efficacy of the product, an initial risk assessment of the critical quality attributes (CQAs - description, identification, uniformity of dosage units, assay, dissolution, impurity) was undertaken, and the CQAs (uniformity of dosage units, assay, and dissolution) that were considered high risk were identified.

All the Material Attributes (MAs) that had the potential to affect the high risk CQAs were identified. Potential critical material attributes (p-CMAs) were identified through risk assessment and experimental studies based on the development knowledge from this product and the final CMAs were identified by further increasing knowledge and understanding. Next, all the Process Parameters (PPs) that have the potential to affect the CMAs were thoroughly clarified. Potential critical process parameters (p-CPPs) were identified through risk assessment and experiments, and the CPPs were identified by increased knowledge and understanding. Management of the CPPs to ensure control of the CMAs within an appropriate range (using process analytical technology (PAT) feedback system in this case) makes it possible to continue to assure the CQAs throughout the product life cycle.

For the CQA of dissolution, the “appropriate ranges” of the CMAs were defined by a design space. In general, process parameters are equipment specific. Considering the equipment specific parameters, in order to continually assure the CQAs to achieve the QTPP, it may be more important to appropriately control CMAs such as uncoated tablet hardness, rather than to control PPs such as compression force within an appropriate range. To meet a “target CMA value,” the feedback control of CPPs, which affect CMAs with PAT, makes it possible to continuously ensure the CQA throughout the product life cycle, and supports the concept of ‘ongoing process verification’, which enables continual improvement. Use of CMAs as input factors makes it possible to manufacture the product to ensure it continually satisfies the QTPP, even when we make changes in manufacturing equipment which have the same operating principle.

1.1 Initial risk assessment and Justification

Description, identification, uniformity of dosage units, assay, impurities and dissolution were identified as CQAs that may need to be controlled to meet the QTPP for Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet, based on the physicochemical properties, the knowledge and information gained through the formulation development and manufacturing experiences. An initial risk assessment assessing the quality of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet was performed for these CQAs using preliminary hazard analysis. The results are shown in Table 1.

Based on the QTPP [[2.3.2.1 Quality Target Product Profile]] for Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet and the results of the initial risk assessment, the uniformity of dosage units was considered high risk, because it is affected by the change in drug substance particle size, blend uniformity, uncoated tablet weight/weight variation, and segregation, and may affect the efficacy and safety in patients.

Assay is considered high risk, because it is affected by the change in uncoated tablet weight and may affect efficacy and safety.

Dissolution was considered high risk, because it is affected by the change in drug substance particle size, physical property of lubricant, granule particle size, lubricity of lubricant at blending, compression force/uncoated tablet hardness, and amount of coating film, and may affect the efficacy and safety.

Among the CQAs, the description is only affected by the coating process, which was confirmed to be acceptable during clinical development and at the process development stages. Due to the low risk of affecting efficacy and safety in patients, description was decided to be controlled as per the specifications. Identification is not affected by variable factors in manufacturing and was considered to have a low risk of affecting efficacy and safety in patients. Thus, identification was decided to be controlled as per the specifications.

It was shown that there was no increase in related substances in formulations during the manufacturing processes, from the excipient compatibility tests and results of clinical tablet manufacturing in the formulations of each strength at the development stages. Therefore, it is considered that drug related impurity content has a low risk of affecting efficacy and safety in patients, provided that the impurities in the drug substance are controlled within the specifications.

1.4 Construction of the control strategy

The relationship between each CMA/CPP, QTPP, and CQA of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet, which was defined in Section 1.2 and Section 1.3, is summarized in Figure 11 in the form of an Ishikawa diagram.

The control strategy to assure each CQA is shown below.

1.4.1 Uniformity of dosage units (CQA)

For the three CMAs affecting uniformity of dosage units (CQA), uncoated tablet weight and uncoated tablet weight variation are determined by in-process control, and granule segregation is monitored by determining drug substance concentrations of the uncoated tablet by an NIR method. If the results exceeded the threshold, Process Analytical Technology (PAT) feedback control, which controls the rotation speed (CPP) is to be employed. As the drug substance concentration of uncoated tablets is determined in 200 or more tablets per batch, RTRT is to be performed in principle.

1.4.2 Assay (CQA)

The CMA of uncoated tablet weight which affects assay (CQA) is to be controlled by in-process control. Because Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet specific CPPs are not present, online monitoring control was employed for the compression force of every tablet through the tableting process, as generally performed. A compression force controller allows correction of the amounts of filled blended powder (filling depth) and removal of tablets out of the acceptable range from the system based on the information of compression force measured. In addition, a correcting system that adjusts the amounts of filled blended powder (filling depth) and compression force control equipment by means of the average weight information periodically measured by automatic sampling and fed back to the tableting machine by weight control equipment is also used. As is the case in uniformity of dosage units, the drug substance concentration of uncoated tablets is determined in 200 or more tablets; thus, RTRT is to be performed using the mean data in principle.

1.4.3 Dissolution (CQA)

The granule particle size is controlled within a certain range in the following ways: 1) Particle size (CMA) of drug substance affecting dissolution (CQA) is a specification item for drug substance, 2) Uncoated tablet hardness (CMA) is controlled by feedback of CPP compression force, 3) Granule particle size (CMA) is monitored using Focused Beam Reflectance Measurement (FBRM), and 4) CPP of spray rate that mostly affects the granule particle size is controlled by PAT feedback.

Regarding uniformity of dosage units and content of drug substance, RTRT is to be performed by determining the drug substance content in uncoated tablets after tableting in principle. On the other hand for dissolution, because a factor controlling CMA covers two or more unit processes, feedforward control can be employed from the upstream to the downstream in the manufacturing process. Thus, dissolution prediction formula can be constructed using three CMA values, and the dissolution is controlled by establishing design space consisting of these three CMA to make feedforward control easy.

Figure 19 Dissolution DoE, central composite design

[IMAGE: Untitled.png]

Dissolution test was performed for the drug product manufactured under the conditions allocated by DoE, and the effect of each factor on the dissolution rate were investigated. The test results were subjected to multidimensional analysis. For the formula for the sum of each factor which is multiplied by a coefficient, the coefficients that make the residual sum of squares minimum were calculated (the formula is shown below).

Dissolution rate = A – B x particle size of drug substance – C x granule particle size – D x uncoated tablet hardness – E × particle size of drug substance × uncoated tablet hardness

To verify the validity of the formula, each CMA (particle size of drug substance, granule particle size, uncoated tablet hardness; refer to Table 11) of the formulation produced at pilot scale (20 kg) and at commercial scale (200 kg) was input into the formula, and the predicted values and the actual values were compared. As a result, as shown in Figure 20, error in prediction, i.e., Root Mean Square Error of Prediction (RMSEP) was 1.6%, showing good agreement. Based on the above results, the formula for dissolution prediction, which was established by DoE at a laboratory scale, was found to be applicable at pilot scale or commercial scale.

1.4.5.3 Overall evaluation of risk assessment

As part of the risk assessment after applying the control strategy, we verified the items that were considered to be low risk at initial risk assessment (Table 1), for those items, no more examination was made.

Description and identification

As shown in sections of [[2.3.4.DP.C Control (Sakura Bloom)[APM][FCT][20 mg]]] and [[2.3.4.DP.S Storage - Bulk (Sakura Bloom )[APM][FCT][20 mg]]], differences in production scale, batch of drug substance, batch of excipients, or manufacturing conditions did not affect the description (appearance) and identification, from the stability test results of clinical tablets and formulations for the pilot scale and the results of manufacture in commercial scale production. It was thus concluded that the effect of manufacturing processes on these attributes was minimal and they have a low risk.

Impurity

For impurity, as shown in sections [[2.3.4.DP.C Control (Sakura Bloom)[APM][FCT][20 mg]]] and [[2.3.4.DP.S Storage - Bulk (Sakura Bloom )[APM][FCT][20 mg]]], related impurities in the drug product were not produced/increased during formulation and storage (including stress testing). It was thus found that the effect of the manufacturing processes on impurity was minimal and they have a low risk.

Uniformity of dosage units and assay

The items that were considered to be low risk at initial risk assessment shown in Table 1, were verified.

• To assess the effect of drug substance on content, we examined the content of the drug product having drug substance with different particle sizes, as shown in Figure 3. As a result, the particle size of drug substance was confirmed not to affect the content.

• To assess the effect of excipients on uniformity of dosage units and assay, the uniformity of dosage units and assay were examined in the drug products manufactured by DoE at each experimental point. As a result, it was confirmed that there were no differences in uniformity of dosage units and assay at all experimental points. Since the formulations for the NDA, which were prepared with even different batches of excipients, and the manufacturing experience on a commercial scale did not matter, it was confirmed that excipients do not affect the uniformity of dosage units and assay.

• The effect of the granulation process on uniformity of dosage units and assay was examined. As shown in 1.2.2 Identification of CMA’ and ‘1.3.2 Identification of CPP,’ it was found that only inappropriate tableting affects the uniformity of dosage units and assay, under the granulation conditions where the drug substance content in each fraction is non-uniform. Since it is obvious that these risks can be controlled by applying the control strategy, they were confirmed to be low risk.

• With respect to the effect of the blending process on content, the blending process was confirmed to have a low risk, because there was no content reduction such as loss of drug substance in the blending process, in any of the drug products shown in this section.

• As for the risk that the coating process affects the uniformity of dosage units and assay, a case was considered where damage or degradation of tablets affects the content in the coating process. However, none of the two cases was observed through the manufacturing experiences and the coating process was confirmed to have a low risk.

Based on the above results, it was verified that the items that were considered to be low risk in the initial risk assessment, following an overall evaluation of the risk assessment, had a low risk.

Conclusions

The data gathered during the process validation show that the manufacturing process of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets is robust and consistently yields drug product which meets the predetermined quality characteristics. Moreover, the chosen in-process tests have been shown to be suitable for monitoring the manufacturing process.

The conclusion from the presented data is that the process conditions and values chosen for the processing parameters are acceptable to support the commercial manufacture of the product.

CQAs of Sakura Bloom Tablets are ensured by CMAs that are maintained by routine production. The control strategy in production of Sakura Bloom Tablets operates the following maintenance program to verify the model.

Daily check:

• Trend analyses of CQA and CMA are performed for every batch produced, and the changes are confirmed to be within an acceptable range.

• If the trend is out of the acceptable level, a comparison is made between the model and conventional testing methods. If the model has some problems, it should be revised. If the model has no problems, the relationship between CPP and CMA is considered to be broken. Thus, control of CPP is reviewed so that CMA has an appropriate value.

Periodical check:

• A comparison is made between the values calculated by the model and those obtained by the conventional testing methods at a certain production interval. If the difference between the two is out of the acceptable level, the model should be revised.

1 Stability Summary and Conclusions

The stability program for Batches 123, 456, and 789 was designed to comprehensively evaluate the product's performance under various environmental conditions to support its registration and commercialization. The study encompassed long-term stability assessments at 25°C/60% RH and 30°C/75% RH over a 36-month period, accelerated stability testing at 40°C/75% RH for up to 6 months, and photostability evaluations to determine sensitivity to light exposure. All data were collected using validated analytical methods and monitored for critical quality attributes such as assay, impurities, dissolution and physical appearance.

1. Assay (% Label Claim)

Across all conditions (25°C/60% RH, 30°C/75% RH, 40°C/75% RH), assay values remain within a tight range: 98.1% to 101.4%. Slight upward trend at 40°C/75% RH, especially in batch ABC789 (up to 101.4%).

While some variability in assay data was reported no stability trend was observed.

Assay remains well within acceptable limits across all conditions. No significant degradation or potency loss observed, even under accelerated conditions.

---

2. Degradation Products (%)

CP-9-1:

Results consistently < 0.10% across all conditions and batches. Occasional detection at 0.10%, but still within specification.

• Mostly Not Detected (ND) or < 0.10%.

Total Impurities:

• Slight increase with temperature:

• 25°C/60% RH: up to 0.11%

Impurity levels are low and stable. Slight increase in total impurities at higher temperatures is expected and within acceptable limits.

---

All batches show dissolution between 94% to 106%. Slight increase in dissolution at 40°C/75% RH, possibly due to enhanced solubility.

Dissolution performance is robust across all conditions. No adverse impact from storage conditions.

---

The bulk Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets are packaged in a primary container consisting of a PETP/AL/PE aluminum composite bag, which is tightly sealed to provide an adequate moisture and oxygen barrier. 2.3.4.DP.S.2 Stability, storage conditions, and shelf life

The stability data generated for Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets stored in PETP/AL/PE composite bags demonstrate that the bulk product remains chemically and physically stable for up to 18 months under long-term storage conditions (25°C/60% RH and 30°C/75% RH). Across both production batches (ABC123 and ABC456), the following results were observed: assay values ranging from 97.4% to 100.9%, total degradation products ranging from 0.2% to 0.4%, unspecified degradation products were consistently reported as <0.2%, and appearance remained unchanged throughout the study period under both conditions. Dissolution after 30 minutes ranged from 92% to 101% (25 °C/60% RH) and 92% to 100% (30 °C/75% RH), meeting the dissolution specification and showing no significant trend. Stability under accelerated conditions (40°C/75% RH) for up to 6 months further supports the stability of the product. Based on these data, a holding time of 18 months is proposed for the bulk product when stored at or below 30°C in tightly sealed PETP/AL/PE bags. These conditions also support intermediate storage and transport under excursions up to 40°C for a limited duration.

The supportive stability study reports for bulk product are provided in [[3.2.DP.S Storage - Bulk (Sakura Bloom) [APM][FCT][20 mg]]].

2.1 Control of related substances

2.1.1 Chiral Purity and Stereoisomer Control Strategy for Sakuramil

The stereoisomeric integrity of CP-4 and consequently of the final drug substance, Sakuramil is controlled to ensure high chiral purity. The first chiral center is introduced via CP-2 (designated as center “A”), a commercially available chiral building block sourced from the chiral pool. The second chiral center (designated as “B”) is established through a well-precedented, highly stereoselective cyclization reaction, yielding the intermediate CP-6.

Figure 1‑2      Chiral Control: Possible Enantiomers and Diastereomers

[IMAGE: attachment:4db2b0e8-dc03-4d55-9ff7-fb1b72ed358b:image.png]

Enantiomer Control

The enantiomeric purity of CP-4 is governed by the enantiomeric specification of CP-2, which is controlled to ≤ 1.5% of the undesired enantiomer in accordance with vendor specification. Any enantiomeric impurity in CP-2 introduced at Step 1 would propagate as CP-9-E, an enantiomeric impurity in the final product. However, CP-9-E has been shown to purge effectively to below 0.10% through downstream crystallization steps involving CP-4, CP-6, CP-7, and Sakuramil.

To further substantiate this control strategy, a development study was conducted in which 5% of the off-enantiomer of CP-2 was deliberately introduced in Step A. The resulting material, processed through the full six-step synthesis, yielded Sakuramil with CP-9-E levels ≤ 0.1%, confirming the robustness of the purge. Information about analytical procedure used is available at [[3.2.AP Analytical Procedures (Enantiomeric impurity)[Purity][Sakuramil]]].

Diastereomer Control

Two theoretical trans diastereomers of CP-9 were considered:

• CP-9-D1: Could hypothetically arise from a disallowed cyclization pathway yielding a trans configuration between centers A and B. However, both experimental data and literature confirm that this pathway is not feasible.

• CP-9-D2: Would require both the incorrect enantiomer of CP-2 and the disallowed cyclization or racemization of center B. These conditions have been thoroughly investigated and ruled out as plausible.

Throughout development, no evidence of racemization at center B in CP-6, CP-7, or Sakuramil has been observed.

Analytical Confirmation and Purge Studies

To confirm the stereochemical control strategy, all three stereoisomers of Sakuramil and selected intermediates were synthesized and analyzed using dedicated, validated analytical methods. All manufactured batches of Sakuramil consistently demonstrated ≤ 0.1% of each stereoisomeric impurity.

No racemization or stereochemical erosion was observed during synthesis development, even under stress conditions applied in Steps 3 and 4. This aligns with literature and mechanistic understanding that both chiral centers are chemically stable and not prone to racemization.

A fate and purge study further demonstrated that spiking CP-6 with 1% of its enantiomer (CP-6-E) and diastereomer (CP-6-D) resulted in <0.1% (below the LOQ of 0.05%) of these impurities in the final drug substance.

2.1.1 Potentially mutagenic impurities

The synthetic route for Sakuramil has been thoroughly evaluated for the presence and control of potentially mutagenic impurities (PMIs), in accordance with ICH M7 guidelines.

(Q)SAR Evaluation and Structural Alerts

Intermediates CP-6 and CP-4 have tested positive in both (Q)SAR systems, indicating potential mutagenic risk. Additionally, non-isolated intermediates CP-3 and CP-5 exhibit structural alerts in structure-activity relationship databases due to the presence of an aniline functionality, which is known to be associated with mutagenic potential.

Figure 1‑3      Potentially mutagenic Intermediates and Reactivity

[IMAGE: attachment:034980fd-c181-404a-a18d-ffd2c87f018f:image.png]

Synthetic Design and Elimination Strategy

The commercial manufacturing process has been strategically designed to mitigate these risks. Specifically, CP-3, CP-5, and CP-6 are all consumed in Step 3 of the synthesis, where the aniline functionality is chemically eliminated. This transformation effectively removes the structural feature responsible for the mutagenic alerts.

Purge and Control Strategy

The reactivity of these intermediates, combined with the hydrophobic nature of downstream products CP-7 and CP-9 (Sakuramil), facilitates efficient purge of residual aniline-containing species. Crystallization steps in both Step 3 and Step 4 further enhance the removal of unreacted anilines and related byproducts.

This integrated control strategy has consistently ensured that PMIs remain within acceptable limits, either under the API specification or within the specifications for starting materials and intermediates.

Supporting Data and Risk Assessment

Comprehensive multivariate development data supporting this control strategy will be presented in this section.Detailed classification of potential and actual impurities according to ICH M7, together with batch results, is presented in [[ICH M7 Risk Assessment]].

2.1.2 Nitrosamine impurities

The synthesis of Sakuramil has been evaluated for the potential formation and presence of nitrosamine impurities, in accordance with current regulatory expectations.

Identified Risk Factors

SM 1 CP-4 contains vulnerable amine. As there is no source of nitrites in Step 1 of Sakuramil manufacturing process there is no risk for formation of corresponding nitrosamine. However, in step 2 CP-5 intermediate, containing vulnerable amine moiety, is converted to CP-6 (also vulnerable amine). In this stage water is used under acidic conditions therefore risk for formation of the corresponding nitrosamines from CP-5 and CP-6 can not be fully excluded. Nevertheless, it is expected that potential nitrosamine of CP-5 would be converted during Step 2 to nitrosamine of CP-6. Therefore, it can be assumed that the levels of nitroso-CP-6, if present, would be significantly higher, than the levels of nitroso-CP-5 and therefore, only nitroso-CP-6 is relevant for further mitigation.

In conclusion, there is a potential risk for nitroso-CP-6 formation in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance, therefore testing of final drug substance batches is needed.

Conclusion and Control Strategy

While the overall nitrosamine risk in the synthesis of Sakuramil is low, the formation of nitroso-CP-6 remains a potential concern.

As a result:

Confirmatory testing of three commercial batches of drug substance for N-Nitroso-CP-6 has been performed. According to the analytical testing results it is demonstrated that the levels of N-nitrosamine impurity are below 10% of acceptable limit.  Therefore, there is no risk for the presence of N-nitrosamine impurity in Sakuramil drug substance and routine testing is not warranted. A detailed assessment, including analysis of risk factors related to manufacturing has been provided in Section 3.2.DS.C

• Nitrosating agents are not expected to be present in the final API.

• CP-6, which contains a secondary amine moiety, is included in the final API specification with a limit of NMT 37.5 ppm.

• Vulnerable amines are present in the final API and are considered in the overall risk assessment and control strategy.

Supporting data and justification will be provided in the multivariate development section and further elaborated in the ICH M7 Risk Assessment ((9+) Nitrosamine Risk Assessment)

1.3.1 Elemental impurities

No metal catalyst is used in Sakuramil DS manufacturing process. Sakuramil DS is evaluated and meets the requirements of ICH Q3D guideline for elemental impurities.

Screening results for Class 1 (Cd, Pb, As and Hg), Class 2A (Co, V and Ni), Class 2B (Pd), Class 3 (Li) and other elements (Mg and B) in Sakuramil drug substance demonstrate that the concentration of elemental impurities is below 30% of the permitted concentration limit for oral administration for all potentially present elements, therefore, no further controls are necessary. Information about the analytical procedure is available at [[3.2.AP Analytical Procedures (Elemental impurities)[Purity][Sakuramil]]].

Magnesium (Mg) and Boron (B) are only mentioned as “Other elements” in the ICH Q3D guideline for elemental impurities. Magnesium is an element that is also widely distributed in plant and animal food. The Permittable Daily Intake of Magnesium is generally considered with 350 mg Mg/day (FNB, 1997). Maximum daily dose of Sakuramil is 60 mg (= 0.06 g). Permitted concentration of Mg is calculated as 5.83 g/g.

The limit for Boron is calculated according to EMA/CHMP/619104/2013. Oral permitted Daily Exposure (PDE) for boron is 9.6 mg B/day. Maximum daily dose of Sakuramil is 60 mg ( = 0.06 g). Permitted concentration of B is calculated as 160 mg/g.

The limits used for the risk assessment represent permitted concentration limits for oral administration in µg/g for elemental impurities in drug substance when Option 1 (according to ICH Q3D) is selected.

2 Risk Assessment

Once the commercial manufacturing process for Sakuramil drug substance was established, increased understanding of the functional relationships between manufacturing process inputs (raw materials, SM, intermediates, etc.) and operating parameters (and their respective levels of criticality) and critical quality attributes of the drug substance was developed. This ultimately led to defining a design space and a control strategy for the manufacturing process.

Initially, a risk assessment process was undertaken to identify potentially critical process parameters and potential scale and equipment dependencies and assess their probable impact on drug substance quality (resulting in an understanding of their criticality and definition of inputs and operating parameters as high risk (critical), moderate risk (key) or low risk (non-critical)). In this risk assessment process, each step of the manufacturing process was considered individually. Firstly, the material attributes of the product for each step were considered with respect to their potential to impact a critical quality attribute of the drug substance. For drug substance processes, this is strictly an impurity exercise until the isolation of the drug substance, where physical characteristic are included. Next, process inputs and process operating parameters for each step were assessed with respect to their potential to impact the important impurity attributes for that step in the process.

This initial structured risk assessment utilized the knowledge that had been gained through development and scale up of the manufacturing process, and a mechanistic and kinetic understanding of the chemistry and the manufacturing process. After identifying the process inputs (raw materials, SM, intermediates, etc.) and process operating parameters and their potential links to drug substance critical quality attributes, an experimental plan was developed, prioritized and executed in order to (a) establish if the identified parameter does impact the quality attributes, and (b) to determine the extent of this impact and identify the design space / proven acceptable ranges (PAR) within which the process can be operated to produce drug substance that meets its specification.

All process-related impurities, including intermediates, diastereomers, and potentially mutagenic compounds, have been identified and assessed throughout the commercial manufacturing process of Sakuramil. CP-6 impurities above 0.1% are controlled based on demonstrated purge capability, and unspecified impurities are limited to NMT 0.1%. The process consistently achieves the desired impurity profile through robust crystallizations, which efficiently purge lipophilic intermediates and impurities.

Key material attributes impacting CQAs include:

• CP-7-1 and CP-9-1, formed in Steps 3 and 4, with low purge and controlled via process parameters.

• Unreacted CP-8, retained in the drug substance, requiring control in Step 4.

• Potentially mutagenic impurities (CP-3, CP-4, CP-5, CP-6) are purged below TTC levels.

• Nitrosamine risk is low due to absence of nitrosating agents, though vulnerable amines are present.

• Chirality is not impacted by the process and remains controlled.

• Residual solvents are effectively removed during crystallization.

• Elemental impurities, such as Pd, are controlled at the SM and intermediate level, with no need for control in the final drug substance.

3 Description of Critical Material Attributes and Critical Process Parameters

3.1 Design space development

A comprehensive design space was established for the Sakuramil manufacturing process based on risk assessments, multivariate experiments, and mechanistic understanding. Focus was placed on Steps 3 and 4, where critical quality attributes (CQAs) are most impacted.

Equivalents (2.0–7.5), sodium carbonate stoichiometry (0.75–4.0), and THF volume (3–15 L/kg), along with crystallization parameters such as cooling rate (0.15–0.5 °C/min), water content (10–50% w/w), ethanol volume (4–10 L/kg), and agitation rate. CP-7-1 remained below the 0.15% specification in all tested conditions, with no edges of failure observed.

In Step 4, residual CP-8 was the primary concern. DoE variables included CP-8 stoichiometry (0.9–2.0 equivalents), phase ratio (NaOH/DCM, 0.25–1.25), reaction concentration (0.25–5 L/kg), cooling rate (0.15–0.5 °C/min), and water content (20–35% w/w). Cooling rate and water content were identified as critical process parameters (CPPs), and when controlled, CP-8 levels remained below 0.10% in the drug substance. Overall, the design space ensures robust control of impurities for Sakuramil drug substance. Further Information on design space development is provided in section [[3 Design Space Development]].

The synthesis of Sakuramil drug substance was evaluated regarding the manufacturing process impact on impurity control. Therefore, CQA of Sakuramil can be controlled by understanding and controlling the formation routes and fate and purge of impurities. The following related substances are found necessary to be controlled in Sakuramil drug substance specification: CP-9-1 with limit NMT 0.15% and CP-8 with limit of NMT 0.10%, meanwhile Individual unspecified impurities are limited at NMT 0.10%.

The identification and control of potentially mutagenic impurities were done according to ICH M7 guideline. An in silico assessment was performed using DEREK Nexus and SARAH Nexus. The following impurities are found to be potentially mutagenic and control strategy was appropriately established in line with control options per ICH M7 guideline.

CP-3, originating from SM CP-4, Class 3, Controlled as per ICH M7 Option 3; CP-3 is included in CP-4 specification with a limit of NMT 0.3%. Carry over results on three final API batches demonstrate levels of CP-3 below 30% of TTC.

CP-4, SM, Class 3, controlled as per ICH M7 Option 3; CP-4 is included in CP-6 specification with a limit of NMT 0.3%. Carry over results on three final API batches demonstrate levels of CP-4 below 30% of TTC.

CP-5, API synthesis, Class 3, controlled as per ICH M7 Option 3; Residual CP-5 is monitored and controlled as Individual unspecified impurity within intermediate CP-6 specification with a limit of NMT 0.1%. Carry over results on three final API batches demonstrate levels of CP-4 below 30% of TTC.

CP-6, API synthesis, Class 3, controlled as per ICH M7 Option 1; included  in Sakuramil drug substance specification with limit of NMT 37.5 ppm

For further details on ICH M7 assessment, please refer to [[ICH M7 Risk Assessment]].

Solvents used in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance are the following : methyl chloroformate, tetrahydrofuran, methanol, ethanol, n-hexane, methylene chloride. Potential residual solvents originating from starting materials are the following: toluene, heptane.Dichloromethane is used in the last step of the synthesis of Sakuramil and only residual dichloromethane is routinely controlled in the drug substance specification with a limit of NMT 600 ppm per ICH Q3C guideline. For all other solvents (ethanol, methanol, n-hexane, tetrahydrofuran, benzene, toluene) carry over results on three API batches  are present demonstrating levels below 10% of the corresponding ICH Q3C limit.

In line with ICH Q3D Guideline for Elemental Impurities, the Risk Assessment was performed in order to identify known and potential sources of elemental impurities in Sakuramil drug substance.

No class 1 elements are intentionally used and hence, not likely to be present in Sakuramil drug substance. Palladium (Pd) – class 2B element - is intentionally added in manufacturing process of SM1 CP-4, controlled in CP4 specification with NMT 10 ppm and therefore also considered in the risk assessment. Lithium (Li) – class 3 element – is intentionally added in form of the reagent Lithium-tert-butoxide. Results of carry over studies according to ICH Q3D guideline are provided in [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]].

1. Excipient controls - Justification of specifications

1.1 Compendial excipients

The excipients used in the formulation of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet are compendial and comply with the references mentioned in Table-1-1 in section [2.3.3. EX].

All compendial excipients comply with the quality requirements of the applicable pharmacopoeial monographs and justification of the compendial specifications is therefore not provided. For the tests appearing in the compendial monograph of the excipients, no re-validation of analytical procedures is deemed necessary.

Adventitious Agents Safety Evaluation

Lactose monohydrate used in Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet is the only excipient of animal origin. The declarations of lactose compliance with EMA Note for guidance on minimizing the risk of transmitting animal spongiform encephalopathy agents via human and veterinary medicinal products, EMA/410/01 rev.3, 2011/C 73/01 are available in Figure 1 and Figure 2 of section [[3.2.EX Compendial excipients]]. Based on the statements provided by the suppliers and to the best of our knowledge, there is no risk of transmitting Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies (TSE) through the excipients.

Additional details pertaining to the lactose monohydrate of animal origin are shared in Table-1 of section [[3.2.EX Compendial excipients]].

1. Excipient controls - Justification of specifications

1.1 Film-coating premix

The basic coating premix red is a combination of ingredients established for use in medicinal products and is commercially available. A monograph for the premix itself does not appear in any pharmacopoeia, however, the ingredients of the basic coating premix red meet compendial requirements and international standards.

The test for total ash, identity by IR and for identity of iron of the basic coating premix red meet the requirements of pharmacopoeia and/or international standards, validation of this analytical procedure is deemed unnecessary. Similarly, validation of analytical procedures performed by visual examination is not deemed necessary.

Reasons for designating CP-4 as regulatory starting material in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil are as follows:

• CP-4 is a significant structural fragment incorporated in the structure of the Sakuramil drug substance.

CP-4 contains the main core structure of Sakuramil: one of the trifluoromethyl as well as the amine residues.

• It is a substance of defined chemical properties and structure.

• CP-4 can be considered as “custom synthesized chemicals” according to ICH Q11 and ICH Q11 Q&A guideline principles.

• Specifications of starting material CP-4 has been well defined to ensure adequate quality of starting material used in the synthesis of Sakuramil drug substance (refer to [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] ).

• Discussion on potential impurities of CP-4, their origin as well as fate and purge are presented within [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]].

• Multiple chemical transformation steps are available between CP-4 and final drug substance.

• In line with all general principles of ICH guideline Q11 on development and manufacture of drug substances (chemical entities and biotechnological/biological entities) and Q&A document.

Manufacturing process (CP-4)

Figure 1-1           Reaction scheme (CP-4, IROHA-corp.)

[IMAGE: Untitled.png]

4-Brom-benzotrifluorid (CP-1) reacts with (3R)-3-Aminohexanenitrile (CP-2) to form in situ intermediate CP-3 in presence of Pd catalyst/ligand as well as base and toluene (Step A). In Step B, Starting Material CP-4 is formed by reacting with concentrated sulphuric acid solution, toluene and heptane.

Figure 1-2           Reaction scheme (CP-4, HETO-corp.)

[IMAGE: Untitled.png]

4-Brom-benzotrifluorid (CP-1) reacts with (3R)-3-Aminohexanenitrile (CP-2) to form CP-3 in presence of Pd catalyst as well as ligand and toluene during temperature heating up to 70°C. In the next step, Starting Material CP-4 is formed by reacting with concentrated sulphuric acid solution and toluene.

Reasons for designating CP-8 as regulatory starting material in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil are as follows:

• CP-8 is a significant structural fragment incorporated in the structure of the Sakuramil drug substance.

CP-8 is a bis-trifluoromethyl benzene side chain incorporated in the structure of the Sakuramil.

• It is a substance of defined chemical properties and structure.

• Starting material CP-8 can be “custom synthesized chemicals” according to ICH Q11 and ICH Q11 Q&A guideline principles.

• Specifications of starting material CP-8 has been well defined to ensure adequate quality of starting materials used in the synthesis of Sakuramil drug substance (refer to [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] ).

• Discussion on potential impurities of CP-8, their origin as well as fate and purge are presented within [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]]

Impurities that are defined to impact the impurity profile of Sakuramil do not originate from earlier steps than of the starting materials. Manufacturing steps upstream of CP-8 are simple.

• Only one chemical transformation step is available between CP-8 and final drug substance. CP-8 is controlled in the drug substance to the level of NMT 0.10%.

• In line with all general principles of ICH guideline Q11 on development and manufacture of drug substances (chemical entities and biotechnological/biological entities) and Q&A document.

action.title: Principle
action.description: The visual comparison of the colour of a film made from both the test substance and in-house reference substance.

action.title: Equipment
action.description: 1.     Device for film production 2.     White cardboard 3.     Propeller-type stirrer or blender

action.title: Procedure
action.description: Dispersion: Disperse 20 mg of test substance in 60 ml of de-ionized water. 15 mL of the dispersion are needed to prepare a film on a UGC-2 card.  Prepare a dispersion also for the in-house reference substance in the same manner.

action.title: Evaluation
action.description: Compare the colour of the film against a film of the in-house reference substance. The test substance is deemed acceptable if the colour of the film matches that of the authentic reference substance.

action.title: Alternative
action.description: The dispersion may also be prepared using an “Eppendorf” reaction vessel and a Vortex with 10 mg of test substance.
